body_md:
Molar mass of $\ce{NH4NO3}$: $2(14.01) + 4(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 80.05$ g/mol.

There are two N atoms per formula unit: $2 \times 14.01 = 28.02$ g.

Mass percent N $= \dfrac{28.02}{80.05} \times 100\% = 35.0\%$.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: both N atoms (28.02 g) divided by the molar mass (80.05 g).
distractor_notes.B: 28.0% is the mass of N in grams per mole, not a percentage of the total.
distractor_notes.C: 17.5% counts only one of the two nitrogen atoms.
distractor_notes.D: 43.7% is roughly the mass percent of H plus N; it double counts.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Find which reagent runs out first.

4.0 mol Al would need $4.0 \times \tfrac{3}{2} = 6.0$ mol $\ce{Cl2}$, but only 5.0 mol is available, so $\ce{Cl2}$ is limiting.

Moles of product from the limiting reagent: $5.0 \text{ mol } \ce{Cl2} \times \dfrac{2 \text{ mol } \ce{AlCl3}}{3 \text{ mol } \ce{Cl2}} = 3.3$ mol.

distractor_notes.A: 4.0 mol assumes Al is limiting; there is not enough chlorine for all the Al.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: chlorine limits, and 5.0 mol Cl2 gives 5.0 × 2/3 = 3.3 mol AlCl3.
distractor_notes.C: 5.0 mol uses a 1:1 ratio between Cl2 and AlCl3; the ratio is 3:2.
distractor_notes.D: 7.5 mol inverts the mole ratio (3/2 instead of 2/3).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Assume 100 g of compound and convert each mass to moles.

C: $54.5 / 12.01 = 4.54$ mol; H: $9.1 / 1.008 = 9.03$ mol; O: $36.4 / 16.00 = 2.28$ mol.

Divide by the smallest (2.28): C 1.99, H 3.97, O 1.00, giving a 2 : 4 : 1 ratio.

Empirical formula: $\ce{C2H4O}$.

distractor_notes.A: CH2O has a 1:2:1 ratio; it would be 40.0% C, not 54.5%.
distractor_notes.B: C3H6O has the same C:H ratio but the wrong O ratio (3:6:1 gives 62.1% C).
distractor_notes.C: C2H5O has an odd H count that does not match 9.1% H (it would be 8.5% H).
distractor_notes.D: Correct: mole ratio 4.54 : 9.03 : 2.28 reduces to 2 : 4 : 1.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O}$, so 2 mol NaOH neutralize 1 mol $\ce{H2SO4}$.

Moles NaOH $= 0.0300 \text{ L} \times 0.200 \text{ M} = 6.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

Moles $\ce{H2SO4} = 6.00 \times 10^{-3} / 2 = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

Concentration $= 3.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol} / 0.0250 \text{ L} = 0.120$ M.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: 6.00 mmol NaOH ÷ 2 = 3.00 mmol acid in 25.0 mL.
distractor_notes.B: 0.167 M inverts the volume ratio (25/30 instead of 30/25) and ignores the 2:1 ratio.
distractor_notes.C: 0.240 M forgets that H2SO4 is diprotic and needs 2 mol NaOH per mole.
distractor_notes.D: 0.060 M divides by 2 twice.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Balanced combustion: $\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$.

Moles $\ce{O2}$ needed $= 2.0 \text{ mol } \ce{C3H8} \times 5 = 10$ mol.

Volume at STP $= 10 \text{ mol} \times 22.4 \text{ L/mol} = 224$ L.

distractor_notes.A: 44.8 L is the volume of the propane itself (2.0 mol), not the oxygen.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: 5 mol O2 per mol C3H8, so 10 mol O2 = 224 L at STP.
distractor_notes.C: 112 L uses 5 mol O2 total instead of 5 mol per mol of propane.
distractor_notes.D: 448 L doubles the answer by applying the factor of 2 twice.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
All C ends up in $\ce{CO2}$ and all H in $\ce{H2O}$.

mol C $= 1.318 / 44.01 = 0.02995$ mol.

mol H $= 2 \times (0.719 / 18.02) = 0.0798$ mol.

Ratio H : C $= 0.0798 / 0.02995 = 2.67 = 8/3$, so the formula is $\ce{C3H8}$.

Check: $0.02995(12.01) + 0.0798(1.008) = 0.440$ g, matching the sample mass.

distractor_notes.A: CH2 comes from rounding 2.67 down to 2; the ratio is 8:3, not 2:1.
distractor_notes.B: C2H5 (ratio 2.5) is close but does not match 2.67.
distractor_notes.C: C3H7 (ratio 2.33) is a bit low; check the factor of 2 for H in H2O.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Only $\ce{NaHCO3}$ decomposes; the mass lost is $\ce{H2O + CO2}$.

Per 2 mol $\ce{NaHCO3}$ (168.0 g), the mass lost is $18.02 + 44.01 = 62.03$ g.

Mass of $\ce{NaHCO3} = 0.620 \text{ g} \times \dfrac{168.0}{62.03} = 1.68$ g.

Mass percent $= 1.68 / 5.00 \times 100\% = 33.6\%$.

distractor_notes.A: 12.4% is the mass loss as a percent of the sample; that is not the NaHCO3 content.
distractor_notes.B: 16.8% uses 84.0 g (1 mol NaHCO3) per 62.0 g lost; two moles of NaHCO3 are needed per mole of H2O and CO2.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: 0.620 g lost × (168.0 g NaHCO3 / 62.03 g lost) = 1.68 g, which is 33.6% of 5.00 g.
distractor_notes.D: 67.2% doubles the correct answer; the 2:1 factor is already in the 168.0 g.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Use the ideal gas law to find moles of $\ce{H2}$ at the stated conditions (not STP).

$n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{(1.00)(0.500)}{(0.08206)(300)} = 0.0203$ mol $\ce{H2}$.

One mole of Zn gives one mole of $\ce{H2}$, so mass Zn $= 0.0203 \times 65.38 = 1.33$ g.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: n = PV/RT at 300 K gives 0.0203 mol, times 65.38 g/mol = 1.33 g.
distractor_notes.B: 1.46 g uses 273 K (STP) instead of the actual 300 K.
distractor_notes.C: 0.665 g halves the answer by applying the 2:1 HCl ratio to zinc.
distractor_notes.D: 2.66 g doubles the answer by using the 2 mol HCl coefficient on zinc.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Combined gas law: $\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$.

$P_2 = P_1 \times \dfrac{V_1}{V_2} \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.00 \times \dfrac{4.00}{2.00} \times \dfrac{450}{300} = 6.00$ atm.

Halving the volume doubles P; raising T by 1.5× multiplies P by 1.5.

distractor_notes.A: 3.00 atm accounts for the temperature increase but not the compression.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: P scales as V1/V2 and T2/T1, giving 2.00 × 2 × 1.5 = 6.00 atm.
distractor_notes.C: 2.67 atm inverts the temperature ratio (300/450).
distractor_notes.D: 1.33 atm inverts both ratios.

author: claude-seed

body_md: $u_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, so at equal $T$, $\dfrac{u_{\ce{H2}}}{u_{\ce{O2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_{\ce{O2}}}{M_{\ce{H2}}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2}} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

distractor_notes.A: 16 is the ratio of molar masses; speed depends on the square root of that ratio.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: the speed ratio is the square root of the inverse molar-mass ratio, √16 = 4.
distractor_notes.C: 2 takes the square root twice (fourth root of 16).
distractor_notes.D: 1/4 inverts the ratio; lighter molecules move faster, not slower.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
All four have similar molar masses (72–74 g/mol), so compare intermolecular forces.

1-Butanol has an O–H group and can hydrogen bond; the others cannot.

Among the rest, pentane (linear) has stronger dispersion forces than compact 2,2-dimethylpropane; diethyl ether is weakly polar but not hydrogen bonded.

Boiling points: 1-butanol (118 °C) > pentane (36 °C) ≈ diethyl ether (35 °C) > 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C).

distractor_notes.A: Pentane relies only on dispersion forces; it boils near 36 °C.
distractor_notes.B: 2,2-Dimethylpropane is the most compact isomer and has the weakest dispersion forces of the group.
distractor_notes.C: Diethyl ether has an O atom but no O–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: hydrogen bonding in 1-butanol dominates at similar molar mass.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{CaCl2}$ dissociates into 3 ions ($\ce{Ca^2+ + 2Cl-}$), so the van't Hoff factor $i = 3$.

$\Delta T_\text{f} = i K_\text{f} m = 3 \times 1.86 \times 0.100 = 0.558$ °C.

Freezing point $= 0 - 0.558 = -0.558$ °C.

distractor_notes.A: −0.186 °C ignores dissociation (i = 1).
distractor_notes.C: −0.372 °C uses i = 2, but CaCl2 gives three ions per formula unit.
distractor_notes.D: −1.86 °C uses a 1 m solution instead of 0.100 m.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Graham's law: $\dfrac{r_\text{unknown}}{r_\text{He}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_\text{He}}{M_\text{unknown}}}$.

$\dfrac{1}{4} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.00}{M}}$, so $\dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{4.00}{M}$ and $M = 64$ g/mol.

$\ce{SO2}$ has molar mass $32.06 + 2(16.00) = 64.1$ g/mol.

distractor_notes.A: CH4 (16 g/mol) would effuse at half the rate of He, not one quarter.
distractor_notes.B: O2 (32 g/mol) would effuse at 1/√8 ≈ 0.35 times the rate of He.
distractor_notes.C: Kr (83.8 g/mol) would be even slower, about 0.22 times.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: rate ratio 1/4 means molar mass ratio 16, so M = 64 g/mol = SO2.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
In an FCC cell, atoms touch along the face diagonal, which has length $a\sqrt{2}$ and spans 4 atomic radii.

$4r = a\sqrt{2}$, so $r = \dfrac{a\sqrt{2}}{4} = \dfrac{a}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{400.}{2.828} = 141$ pm.

distractor_notes.A: 200 pm assumes atoms touch along the edge (simple cubic, r = a/2).
distractor_notes.B: 173 pm uses the body diagonal (BCC relation r = a√3/4).
distractor_notes.C: Correct: FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal, r = a√2/4 = 141 pm.
distractor_notes.D: 283 pm is a/√2, the distance between adjacent atoms (2r), not the radius.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Convert pressure: $7.60 \text{ torr} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ atm}}{760 \text{ torr}} = 0.0100$ atm.

$\Pi = MRT \Rightarrow M = \dfrac{0.0100}{(0.08206)(300)} = 4.06 \times 10^{-4}$ mol/L.

Moles in 0.1000 L: $4.06 \times 10^{-5}$ mol.

Molar mass $= \dfrac{2.00 \text{ g}}{4.06 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}} = 4.9 \times 10^4$ g/mol.

distractor_notes.A: 4.9 × 10³ uses 1.00 L instead of 0.100 L of solution.
distractor_notes.B: 4.5 × 10⁴ uses 273 K instead of 300 K.
distractor_notes.C: 4.9 × 10⁵ misplaces the decimal in the torr-to-atm conversion.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: Π = 0.0100 atm gives 4.06 × 10⁻⁵ mol in 100 mL, so M ≈ 4.9 × 10⁴ g/mol.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The constant $a$ grows with the strength of intermolecular attractions.

He is a small nonpolar atom with very weak dispersion forces (smallest $a$).

$\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ are nonpolar; $\ce{CO2}$ has more electrons and larger dispersion forces.

$\ce{NH3}$ is polar and hydrogen bonds, giving the strongest attractions and the largest $a$ (about 4.2 L²·atm/mol², versus 3.6 for $\ce{CO2}$).

distractor_notes.A: He has the weakest attractions of any gas; its a is nearly zero.
distractor_notes.B: N2 is nonpolar and small; its a is small (about 1.4).
distractor_notes.C: Correct: NH3 hydrogen bonds, so its attractive correction is largest.
distractor_notes.D: CO2 has sizeable dispersion forces but is nonpolar; its a is smaller than that of NH3.

concept_ref: Real gases and the van der Waals equation
author: claude-seed

body_md:
Keep the first equation; reverse the second so $\ce{CO}$ appears as a product.

$\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}$: $\Delta H = -393.5$ kJ

$\ce{CO2 -> CO + 1/2 O2}$: $\Delta H = +283.0$ kJ

Add: $\ce{C + 1/2 O2 -> CO}$, $\Delta H = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5$ kJ.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ after reversing the second equation.
distractor_notes.B: +110.5 kJ has the sign backwards; forming CO from its elements is exothermic.
distractor_notes.C: −676.5 kJ adds the two equations without reversing the second.
distractor_notes.D: −221.0 kJ doubles the answer, as if two moles of CO formed.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Heat absorbed by the water: $q = m c \Delta T = 500. \times 4.184 \times 5.00 = 10{,}460$ J $= 10.46$ kJ.

That heat came from 2.00 g of fuel, so the heat of combustion is $10.46 / 2.00 = 5.23$ kJ/g.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: q = 500 × 4.184 × 5.00 = 10.46 kJ, divided by 2.00 g.
distractor_notes.B: 10.5 kJ/g is the total heat, not divided by the 2.00 g of fuel.
distractor_notes.C: 2.09 kJ/g uses a 2.00 °C rise instead of 5.00 °C.
distractor_notes.D: 20.9 kJ/g multiplies by the sample mass instead of dividing.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Entropy increases when the number of gas molecules increases or when a substance moves toward a more disordered phase.

Only the decomposition of $\ce{CaCO3}$ produces gas from a solid (0 → 1 mol gas), so its $\Delta S > 0$.

The other three all decrease disorder: fewer gas moles (A, C) or liquid → solid (B).

distractor_notes.A: 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas: entropy decreases.
distractor_notes.B: Freezing produces an ordered solid: entropy decreases.
distractor_notes.C: 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas: entropy decreases.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: a solid releases a gas, so entropy increases.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. With $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$, the enthalpy term favors the reaction and the entropy term opposes it.

At low $T$ the $-T\Delta S$ term is small, so $\Delta G < 0$; at high $T$ the positive $-T\Delta S$ term dominates and $\Delta G > 0$.

The crossover is at $T = \Delta H / \Delta S = 92{,}000 / 199 \approx 460$ K.

distractor_notes.A: Spontaneous at all T requires ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: negative ΔH and negative ΔS give ΔG < 0 only below about 460 K.
distractor_notes.C: High T favors reactions with ΔS > 0, but here ΔS is negative.
distractor_notes.D: Never spontaneous requires ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\Delta H \approx \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed})$.

Broken: one H–H (436) + one Cl–Cl (243) $= 679$ kJ.

Formed: two H–Cl $= 2 \times 432 = 864$ kJ.

$\Delta H = 679 - 864 = -185$ kJ.

distractor_notes.A: +185 kJ subtracts in the wrong order (formed minus broken).
distractor_notes.B: −247 kJ counts only one H–Cl bond formed instead of two.
distractor_notes.D: −617 kJ subtracts only the Cl–Cl energy from the bonds formed.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K$.

$\ln(1.0 \times 10^{5}) = 5 \times 2.303 = 11.51$.

$\Delta G^\circ = -(8.314)(298)(11.51) = -2.85 \times 10^{4}$ J/mol $= -28.5$ kJ/mol.

A large $K$ corresponds to a negative $\Delta G^\circ$.

distractor_notes.B: +28.5 kJ/mol has the wrong sign; K > 1 means products are favored and ΔG° < 0.
distractor_notes.C: −12.4 kJ/mol uses log10 K (5.0) instead of ln K (11.5).
distractor_notes.D: −285 kJ/mol is off by a factor of ten in the unit conversion.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
At the normal boiling point, liquid and vapor are in equilibrium, so $\Delta G_\text{vap} = 0$.

$0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \dfrac{40{,}700 \text{ J/mol}}{109 \text{ J/(mol·K)}} = 373$ K.

These are the values for water, which boils at 373 K.

distractor_notes.A: 273 K is the freezing point of water, not the result of ΔH/ΔS.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: T = ΔH/ΔS = 40,700/109 = 373 K.
distractor_notes.C: 0.373 K forgets to convert kJ to J.
distractor_notes.D: 4.44 K multiplies ΔS by ΔH instead of dividing (in mismatched units).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta(PV) = \Delta U + \Delta n_\text{gas} RT$ for ideal gases.

$\Delta n_\text{gas} = 2 - (1 + 3) = -2$.

$\Delta n RT = (-2)(8.314)(298) = -4.96 \times 10^{3}$ J $= -4.96$ kJ.

$\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n RT = -92.2 - (-4.96) = -87.2$ kJ.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: ΔU = ΔH − ΔnRT with Δn = −2 gives −92.2 + 4.96 = −87.2 kJ.
distractor_notes.B: −92.2 kJ assumes ΔU = ΔH, which is only true when Δn(gas) = 0.
distractor_notes.C: −82.3 kJ uses Δn = −4 (counts only reactant gas moles).
distractor_notes.D: −97.2 kJ subtracts 4.96 kJ instead of adding it (sign of Δn).

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Compare trials that change one concentration at a time.

Trials 1 → 2: [A] doubles, rate goes ×4, so the order in A is 2.

Trials 1 → 3: [B] doubles, rate goes ×2, so the order in B is 1.

Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^2[\ce{B}]$.

distractor_notes.A: First order in A would only double the rate when [A] doubles, but it quadrupled.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: rate ×4 for doubling [A] (second order) and ×2 for doubling [B] (first order).
distractor_notes.C: This swaps the orders; it is [A] that gives the ×4 response.
distractor_notes.D: Second order in B would quadruple the rate in trial 3; it only doubled.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Radioactive decay is first order, so each half-life halves the amount.

90.0 min is three half-lives: $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{8} = 12.5\%$.

distractor_notes.A: 33% treats the decay as linear (90 min is 3 half-lives, not one third gone).
distractor_notes.B: Correct: three half-lives leave (1/2)³ = 1/8 = 12.5%.
distractor_notes.C: 6.25% is four half-lives (120 min).
distractor_notes.D: 25% is two half-lives (60 min), not three.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The Arrhenius equation $k = A e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ shows that $k$ depends on temperature through the exponential factor, which is the fraction of collisions with energy $\ge E_\text{a}$.

Collision frequency rises only as $\sqrt{T}$ (a few percent per 10 °C), far too little to explain the typical doubling of rate.

$E_\text{a}$ itself is a property of the reaction pathway and does not change with temperature.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: the Boltzmann fraction exp(−Ea/RT) rises steeply with T.
distractor_notes.B: Equilibrium position is a thermodynamic question and is unrelated to how fast the reaction proceeds.
distractor_notes.C: Activation energy is fixed by the mechanism; temperature does not change it (a catalyst does).
distractor_notes.D: Collision frequency scales with √T and increases only a few percent per 10 °C.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The rate law is set by the slow (rate-determining) step.

Step 1 is bimolecular in $\ce{NO2}$, so rate $= k[\ce{NO2}]^2$.

$\ce{CO}$ only appears after the slow step, so its concentration does not affect the rate; $\ce{NO3}$ is an intermediate and cannot appear in the overall rate law.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: the slow step involves two NO2 molecules.
distractor_notes.B: This is the rate law of the overall equation, but rate laws come from the mechanism, not the stoichiometry.
distractor_notes.C: CO participates only in the fast step, so it does not appear.
distractor_notes.D: NO3 is an intermediate; intermediates are not written in the rate law.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
On a reaction coordinate diagram, the transition state sits 75 kJ/mol above the reactants and the products sit 40 kJ/mol below the reactants.

$E_\text{a,reverse} = E_\text{a,forward} - \Delta H = 75 - (-40) = 115$ kJ/mol.

For an exothermic reaction the reverse barrier is always larger than the forward one.

distractor_notes.A: 35 kJ/mol subtracts 40 instead of adding; the products are below the reactants, so the reverse climb is longer.
distractor_notes.B: 40 kJ/mol is the magnitude of ΔH, not a barrier.
distractor_notes.C: 75 kJ/mol is the forward barrier; the reverse differs by ΔH.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: Ea(rev) = Ea(fwd) − ΔH = 75 + 40 = 115 kJ/mol.

author: claude-seed

distractor_notes.A: 0.0677 M uses the first-order law [A] = [A]0·e^(−kt).
distractor_notes.B: 0.125 M applies two half-lives, but second-order half-lives are not constant.
distractor_notes.D: 0.400 M uses a zero-order law [A] = [A]0 − kt with the wrong units.

body_md:
Two-temperature Arrhenius form: $\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$.

$\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{310} = \dfrac{10}{93{,}000} = 1.075 \times 10^{-4}$ K$^{-1}$.

$E_\text{a} = \dfrac{R \ln 2}{1.075 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{(8.314)(0.693)}{1.075 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.36 \times 10^{4}$ J/mol $\approx 54$ kJ/mol.

distractor_notes.A: 5.4 kJ/mol is off by a factor of ten (misplaced decimal in 1/T1 − 1/T2).
distractor_notes.B: 27 kJ/mol uses log10 2 (0.301) instead of ln 2 (0.693).
distractor_notes.C: 107 kJ/mol doubles the answer (ln 4 instead of ln 2).
distractor_notes.D: Correct: Ea = R ln 2 / (1/300 − 1/310) ≈ 54 kJ/mol.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
The slow step gives rate $= k_2[\ce{N2O2}][\ce{O2}]$, but $\ce{N2O2}$ is an intermediate and must be eliminated.

Step 1 is a fast equilibrium: $K_1 = \dfrac{[\ce{N2O2}]}{[\ce{NO}]^2}$, so $[\ce{N2O2}] = K_1[\ce{NO}]^2$.

Substituting: rate $= k_2 K_1 [\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}] = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}]$.

distractor_notes.A: This is the slow-step rate law before eliminating the intermediate N2O2.
distractor_notes.B: This ignores the O2 in the slow step.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: substituting [N2O2] = K1[NO]² into the slow step gives k[NO]²[O2].
distractor_notes.D: This treats the overall reaction as elementary with the wrong coefficients.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Le Chatelier's principle: the system shifts to counteract a change.

The reaction is exothermic, so lowering $T$ favors the forward (heat-producing) direction.

There are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so raising $P$ favors the side with fewer gas moles: products.

A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not change the equilibrium position.

distractor_notes.A: Higher T and lower P both push the equilibrium toward reactants.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: low temperature favors the exothermic direction; high pressure favors fewer gas moles.
distractor_notes.C: A catalyst changes the rate, not the position, of equilibrium.
distractor_notes.D: Removing a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward reactants, lowering NH3.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$K_\text{p} = K_\text{c}(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ is the change in moles of gas.

$\Delta n = 2 - 1 = 1$.

$K_\text{p} = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \times (0.08206 \times 298)^{1} = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 24.5 = 0.11$.

distractor_notes.A: 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ divides by RT instead of multiplying (Δn = −1).
distractor_notes.B: Kp equals Kc only when Δn = 0; here Δn = 1.
distractor_notes.D: 2.8 uses (RT)² (Δn = 2), counting only the product side.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{Ag2CrO4(s) <=> 2Ag+(aq) + CrO4^2-(aq)}$. If the solubility is $s$, then $[\ce{Ag+}] = 2s$ and $[\ce{CrO4^2-}] = s$.

$K_\text{sp} = (2s)^2(s) = 4s^3 = 1.1 \times 10^{-12}$.

$s^3 = 2.75 \times 10^{-13}$, so $s = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ M.

distractor_notes.A: Correct: 4s³ = Ksp gives s = (2.75 × 10⁻¹³)^(1/3) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
distractor_notes.B: 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ M is √Ksp, which applies only to 1:1 salts.
distractor_notes.C: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M is the cube root of Ksp without the factor of 4 from (2s)².
distractor_notes.D: 5.5 × 10⁻¹³ M is Ksp/2, not a solubility.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
$\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}$; let $x = [\ce{H+}]$.

$K_\text{a} = \dfrac{x^2}{0.10 - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{0.10} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$.

$x^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$, so $x = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M and pH $= 3.00$.

The approximation holds because $x$ is 1% of 0.10 M.

distractor_notes.A: pH 1.00 treats the acid as strong (fully dissociated).
distractor_notes.B: pH 2.50 is −log(√Ka) with the concentration left out.
distractor_notes.D: pH 5.00 is pKa, which is the pH only when [HA] = [A−].

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH $= \text{p}K_\text{a} + \log\dfrac{[\ce{A-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}$.

pH $= 4.74 + \log 10 = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74$.

More conjugate base than acid pushes the pH above p$K_\text{a}$.

distractor_notes.A: 3.74 subtracts the log term; more base means higher pH, not lower.
distractor_notes.B: 4.74 is the pH only when the acid and base concentrations are equal.
distractor_notes.C: Correct: pH = pKa + log(10) = 5.74.
distractor_notes.D: 6.74 adds 2, which would require a 100:1 ratio.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
ICE: $[\ce{H2}] = [\ce{I2}] = 1.00 - x$, $[\ce{HI}] = 2x$.

$K_\text{c} = \dfrac{(2x)^2}{(1.00 - x)^2} = 64$.

Take the square root of both sides: $\dfrac{2x}{1.00 - x} = 8$, so $2x = 8 - 8x$ and $x = 0.80$ M.

$[\ce{HI}] = 2x = 1.60$ M.

distractor_notes.A: 0.80 M is x, but [HI] = 2x.
distractor_notes.B: 0.89 M drops the coefficient 2 in the ICE table and reports x.
distractor_notes.C: 1.78 M drops the coefficient 2 when solving but then doubles at the end.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: 2x/(1 − x) = 8 gives x = 0.80, so [HI] = 1.60 M.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
At equivalence, all the acid has become acetate; the solution volume is 50.0 mL.

$[\ce{CH3COO-}] = 2.50 \text{ mmol} / 50.0 \text{ mL} = 0.0500$ M.

Acetate is a weak base: $K_\text{b} = K_\text{w}/K_\text{a} = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} / 1.8 \times 10^{-5} = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$.

$[\ce{OH-}] = \sqrt{K_\text{b} \times 0.0500} = \sqrt{2.8 \times 10^{-11}} = 5.3 \times 10^{-6}$ M.

pOH $= 5.28$, so pH $= 14.00 - 5.28 = 8.72$.

distractor_notes.A: pH 7.00 is the equivalence point only for a strong acid–strong base titration.
distractor_notes.B: Correct: the acetate hydrolyzes at 0.0500 M, giving pOH 5.28 and pH 8.72.
distractor_notes.C: 8.87 forgets the dilution and uses 0.100 M acetate.
distractor_notes.D: 5.28 is the pOH, not the pH.

author: claude-seed

body_md:
Add the two equilibria: $\ce{AgCl(s) + 2NH3 <=> [Ag(NH3)2]+ + Cl-}$, with $K = K_\text{sp} K_\text{f} = (1.8 \times 10^{-10})(1.6 \times 10^{7}) = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$.

Let $s$ = solubility: $[\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}] = [\ce{Cl-}] = s$ and $[\ce{NH3}] = 1.0 - 2s$.

$K = \dfrac{s^2}{(1.0 - 2s)^2}$; take the square root: $\dfrac{s}{1.0 - 2s} = 0.054$.

$s = 0.054(1.0 - 2s) \Rightarrow s(1 + 0.108) = 0.054 \Rightarrow s = 4.8 \times 10^{-2}$ M.

distractor_notes.A: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water (√Ksp), ignoring complex formation.
distractor_notes.B: 2.9 × 10⁻³ M is the overall K itself, not the solubility.
distractor_notes.C: 5.4 × 10⁻² M ignores the NH3 consumed (2 mol per Ag+), a 10% error.
distractor_notes.D: Correct: √(Ksp·Kf) = s/(1 − 2s) gives s = 0.048 M.
